chapter_title: Integrating with WalletConnect and Multi-chain Support

screens.title: Integrating WalletConnect & Multi‑chain Support
screens.subtitle: Secure cross‑device wallet connections and strategies for supporting multiple EVM chains

narration.text: In this lesson we will learn why WalletConnect matters and how multi‑chain support changes the way you build dApps. WalletConnect is a lightweight open protocol that bridges dApps to mobile and desktop wallets using QR codes and deep links. That bridge preserves user key security while letting your application request signatures and transactions from a remote wallet. Multi‑chain support means your dApp can detect which blockchain a user is on, switch networks when needed, and load the correct contract addresses and RPC endpoints. Practically, you will see how to install a WalletConnect provider, enable a session, and listen for accounts and chain changes. You will also see the common pattern for switching networks and handling the case where a chain is not yet added to the user's wallet. By the end of this chapter you will be able to connect both MetaMask and WalletConnect users, present clear network state to users, and adapt contract interactions per chain. Consider a user who wants to move from Sepolia to Mumbai: your dApp must both ask the wallet to switch networks and then reinitialize the contract instance for the target chain. Keep that pattern in mind as a core design principle.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Use WalletConnect as a secure bridge for mobile/desktop wallets; treat chainId as the single source of truth for loading contracts and RPCs.

narration.text: Over the next screens you will gain four concrete skills that make your dApp more accessible and reliable. First, you will understand what WalletConnect is and how its session model securely connects a browser dApp with mobile wallets using QR codes and deep links. Practically, this means your application can trigger a request and receive signatures without ever storing private keys. Second, you will be able to implement WalletConnect in a React app and wire it into Web3. js. You will learn provider configuration, enabling a session, and listening for provider events so your UI stays in sync. Third, you will learn how multi‑chain dApps detect and respond to chainId. You will read chainId, display network names, and load chain‑specific RPCs and contract addresses. Fourth, you will implement network switching and handle the common error where the wallet does not have a requested chain; you will learn to add the chain using wallet_addEthereumChain when needed. Each objective includes a short milestone you can verify by running the supplied component and switching between Sepolia and Mumbai testnets. These skills help you reach verified competency by enabling mobile wallet users, reducing failed transactions, and supporting a larger user base across multiple chains.

screens.title: What is WalletConnect?
screens.subtitle: A secure bridge between dApps and external wallets

narration.text: WalletConnect is an open protocol that creates an encrypted session between a dApp and a wallet. Conceptually, treat it as a tunnel: the dApp sends JSON‑RPC requests over the tunnel, and the wallet responds with signed messages or transaction approvals. The critical security property is that private keys remain inside the wallet; the dApp never receives raw keys. As a concrete example, a desktop dApp shows a QR code. A mobile wallet scans it and establishes a session; the dApp can then ask the wallet to sign a transaction and the wallet asks the user to confirm. A common misconception is that WalletConnect transfers keys or gives the dApp account control. It doesn't; it merely requests actions that the wallet signs on behalf of the user. Another important point is provider abstraction: libraries such as @walletconnect/web3-provider or web3modal wrap the protocol and present a regular web3 provider object your code can use. That means your existing Web3. js or Ethers. js flows for sending transactions and reading chain state work with minimal changes. Key takeaway: think of WalletConnect as a remote signer and session manager, not a replacement for your provider logic. How will you design your UI to make clear when a session is active and which wallet is connected?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: WalletConnect is an encrypted session protocol — it requests signatures from remote wallets without exposing private keys.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › What is WalletConnect?
Core Concept

WalletConnect as a secure bridge

WalletConnect opens an encrypted channel so the dApp can request signatures while keys remain in the user's wallet. It's used for QR codes and deep links.

Analogy
Think of WalletConnect as a courier carrying approved paperwork between your dApp and a locked safe where keys are kept.
Concrete example
A desktop dApp shows QR; mobile wallet scans; dApp requests a transaction signature; wallet prompts user to approve.
Common misconception
WalletConnect does not export keys. It only transmits requests and signed responses over an encrypted session.
Provider abstraction
Use libraries like @walletconnect/web3-provider to wrap WalletConnect as a Web3 provider. That lets existing code call web3.eth.getAccounts, web3.eth.sendTransaction, and other familiar APIs.
Key takeaway
Key Takeaway

Treat WalletConnect as a remote signer and a session manager; preserve existing provider logic and update only the provider instance.

screens.title: How a WalletConnect session is established
screens.subtitle: From QR code to an encrypted provider session

narration.text: A WalletConnect session follows a predictable sequence you will implement inside your dApp. First, the dApp constructs a provider instance with necessary configuration such as an Infura project ID and an RPC map for any chains you plan to support. Next, the dApp calls enable() on the provider. That triggers the QR code flow for desktop or a deep link on mobile. When the wallet scans or follows the link, both ends exchange handshake messages and negotiate an encrypted channel. At this point the provider exposes standard web3 methods and the dApp can call getAccounts and read the chainId. Example: after calling provider. enable(), create const web3 = new Web3(provider) and call web3. eth. getAccounts() to get the connected address. Important events include accountsChanged, chainChanged, and disconnect — you must listen and react to them. A common pitfall is assuming the session will persist without handling disconnect: always clear app state and possibly prompt reconnection on disconnect. Final takeaway: the session pattern is initialization, enable, handshake, then subscribe to events. Think about how your UI communicates session state clearly to prevent user confusion.

keyIdea.title: Session steps
keyIdea.text: Initialize provider with Infura/RPCs → enable() to start handshake → create web3 instance → subscribe to provider events.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Session Flow
Process

Establishing a WalletConnect session

  1. Configure provider with Infura ID and RPC map for supported chains.
  2. Call provider.enable() to trigger QR or deep link flow and complete handshake.
  3. Create a Web3 instance: const web3 = new Web3(provider).
  4. Read accounts and chainId, then subscribe to accountsChanged, chainChanged, disconnect.
Example code
import WalletConnectProvider from '@walletconnect/web3-provider';
import Web3 from 'web3';

const provider = new WalletConnectProvider({
  infuraId: 'YOUR_INFURA_PROJECT_ID',
  rpc: { 1: 'https://mainnet.infura.io/v3/YOUR_INFURA_PROJECT_ID', 137: 'https://polygon-rpc.com' }
});

await provider.enable();
const web3 = new Web3(provider);
const accounts = await web3.eth.getAccounts();
What to watch for
  • Make sure the Infura ID is configured; without it WalletConnect cannot reach nodes for some chains.
  • Always register event listeners to keep UI state in sync when accounts or chain change.
  • Clear session and reset state on disconnect; don’t rely on the provider to auto‑reconnect.
Key Takeaway

The enable() handshake creates an encrypted provider; treat it like any provider and listen for lifecycle events.

screens.title: Integrating WalletConnect in React
screens.subtitle: Provider configuration, enable(), and event wiring

narration.text: Integrating WalletConnect in React is a matter of creating and managing a provider instance, wrapping it with Web3, and wiring event listeners into component state. Start by installing @walletconnect/web3-provider and web3. Configure the provider with an Infura project ID and an RPC map for networks you plan to support. In a component, call await provider. enable() and then const web3 = new Web3(provider). After that, read web3. eth. getAccounts() and web3. eth. getChainId() to set the connected account and the active chain. Important events are accountsChanged, chainChanged, and disconnect — attach handlers that update state and remove listeners on cleanup to avoid memory leaks. A typical mistake is to treat provider. enable() as a one‑time synchronous operation; it prompts the external wallet and may reject or time out, so wrap it in try/catch and surface a clear status message. Also remember MetaMask and WalletConnect expose different connection mechanics: MetaMask uses window. ethereum while WalletConnect uses a remote provider object. Your component should support both providers and normalize events so the rest of your app deals with a single source of truth for account and chainId. Finally, always reinitialize contract instances after a chain change.

keyIdea.title: Integration pattern
keyIdea.text: Create provider → enable() → new Web3(provider) → read accounts/chainId → subscribe to events and reinitialize contracts on chain changes.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › React Integration
Code Walkthrough

Provider setup and enable

// Provider config
import WalletConnectProvider from '@walletconnect/web3-provider';
import Web3 from 'web3';

const provider = new WalletConnectProvider({
  infuraId: 'YOUR_INFURA_PROJECT_ID',
  rpc: {
    11155111: 'https://sepolia.infura.io/v3/YOUR_INFURA_PROJECT_ID',
    80001: 'https://rpc-mumbai.maticvigil.com'
  }
});

// Enable and create web3
try {
  await provider.enable();
  const web3 = new Web3(provider);
  const accounts = await web3.eth.getAccounts();
  const chainId = await web3.eth.getChainId();
} catch (err) {
  console.error('Connection failed:', err);
}
Event wiring
  • provider.on('accountsChanged', handler) — update account state or disconnect if none.
  • provider.on('chainChanged', handler) — parse hex or decimal, update chainId, reload contracts.
  • provider.on('disconnect', handler) — cleanup and clear session.
Common mistake

Not removing event listeners or not handling promise rejections from enable() causes stale UI and confusing errors.

Key Takeaway

Normalize provider behavior across MetaMask and WalletConnect so the rest of the app consumes a single account and chain state.

screens.title: Detecting chainId and showing network info
screens.subtitle: Why chainId is the single source of truth for multi‑chain dApps

narration.text: Chain ID is the single reliable identifier for the blockchain network the wallet is currently using. When a user connects, call web3. eth. getChainId() or listen for chainChanged events; both return the active chain ID. Display this to the user as a network name so they know where transactions will execute. For example, chainId 11155111 corresponds to Sepolia testnet; 80001 corresponds to Mumbai testnet. Do not hardcode logic to assume Ethereum Mainnet — many users will operate on L2s and testnets. A common error is using chain names in code logic; names can vary so map chainId to your internal configuration. After detecting chainId, load the appropriate RPC endpoint, native currency label, and contract address from a configuration object. In practice: when chainChanged fires, parse the payload (hex or decimal), set your chain state, then reinitialize web3. eth. Contract instances with the contract address for that chain. Takeaway: treat chainId as authoritative and reinitialize any chain‑specific resources whenever it changes. Detecting chainId and showing network info means always use chainid as authoritative. map chainid to rpcs, native currency, and contract addresses and reload resources on change.. In practical terms, why chainid is the single source of truth for multi‑chain dapps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Chain detection
keyIdea.text: Always use chainId as authoritative. Map chainId to RPCs, native currency, and contract addresses and reload resources on change.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Detect chainId
Definition

chainId is authoritative

Use web3.eth.getChainId() or subscribe to chainChanged events to determine the network. Map the numeric chainId to your network configuration to select RPC, explorer, and contract addresses.

Configuration pattern
const NETWORKS = {
  11155111: { name: 'Sepolia Testnet', rpcUrl: 'https://sepolia.infura.io/v3/ID' },
  80001: { name: 'Polygon Mumbai', rpcUrl: 'https://rpc-mumbai.maticvigil.com' }
};
UX guidance
  • Always show the current network name derived from chainId so users know where transactions will run.
  • If a required contract is not deployed on the active chain, show a clear message and offer a network switch option.
  • Do not assume a particular chain — make your logic chainId-driven.
Key Takeaway

Use chainId as the single source of truth and reload chain‑specific resources when it changes.

screens.title: Requesting a network switch and handling errors
screens.subtitle: Using wallet_switchEthereumChain and wallet_addEthereumChain when needed

narration.text: When your dApp needs the user to move to a specific chain, call the RPC method wallet_switchEthereumChain with the chain ID in hex form. For MetaMask this is a request on window. ethereum; for WalletConnect providers you call provider. request. Wrap the call in a try/catch. If the wallet throws error code 4902, that means the wallet doesn't have the chain configured. Your dApp can then call wallet_addEthereumChain with the chain parameters — RPC URL, chain name, native currency, and explorer values — and then attempt the switch again. A concrete example: if the user is on Sepolia but your feature requires Mumbai, call wallet_switchEthereumChain with Mumbai's hex ID. If 4902 is returned, call wallet_addEthereumChain with Mumbai's network object, then reattempt the switch. A common pitfall is not gracefully surfacing these steps: always present clear user feedback and handle rejection scenarios where the user declines to add or switch networks. After a successful switch, update state and reinitialize contract instances. Final question: how will your UI explain why the user must switch and what changing networks will do for their transaction?

keyIdea.title: Network switching
keyIdea.text: Request wallet_switchEthereumChain; on 4902 call wallet_addEthereumChain with network parameters and retry the switch.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Switch Networks
RPC Methods
Use wallet_switchEthereumChain to request switching. If error code 4902 appears, the wallet lacks the chain and you should call wallet_addEthereumChain with the network object and then retry.
Example flow
try {
  await provider.request({ method: 'wallet_switchEthereumChain', params: [{ chainId: '0x13881' }] });
} catch (switchError) {
  if (switchError.code === 4902) {
    await provider.request({ method: 'wallet_addEthereumChain', params: [{ /* network params */ }] });
    // retry switch
  }
}
UX and error handling
  • Inform users why the network change is necessary before prompting the wallet.
  • Handle user rejection of add or switch gracefully, with a clear recovery path.
  • After switching, reload contracts and refresh network‑dependent UI elements.
Common mistake

Treating chain switch as guaranteed; always handle 4902 and rejection flows and do not proceed until chainChanged confirms the new chain.

screens.title: Managing contract addresses across chains
screens.subtitle: Configuration patterns and safe contract initialization

narration.text: Contracts are deployed to specific chains; the same contract address on one chain is not valid on another. To support multi‑chain interactions, maintain a configuration object that maps chainId to contract addresses and any chain‑specific data such as native currency or RPC endpoints. When the active chain changes, your app must select the right address and reinitialize the web3. eth. Contract instance with that address and the ABI. A safe pattern is to centralize this mapping in a module named contractConfig and expose a function getContractAddress(chainId). For example, CONTRACT_ADDRESSES[137] returns the Polygon address. After the chain change event, call new web3. eth. Contract(ABI, getContractAddress(chainId)). A frequent error is keeping a single contract object and forgetting to update it after a chain switch — that causes transactions to target the wrong chain or fail entirely. Another nuance: some functionality or bridges may be chain specific; gate those features behind checks for the active chainId. Final takeaway: treat contract instances as ephemeral and bound to the active chain; reinstantiate after every chain change to avoid mismatches. Managing contract addresses across chains means map contract addresses to chainid and reinitialize contract instances whenever the chain changes to ensure correct interactions.. In practical terms, configuration patterns and safe contract initialization. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Contract mapping
keyIdea.text: Map contract addresses to chainId and reinitialize contract instances whenever the chain changes to ensure correct interactions.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Contract Management
Hierarchy

Contract configuration pattern

const CONTRACT_ADDRESSES = {
  1: '0x...MainnetContract...',
  137: '0x...PolygonContract...',
  42161: '0x...ArbitrumContract...'
};

function getContractAddress(chainId) {
  return CONTRACT_ADDRESSES[chainId];
}
Reinitialize after chain changes: const contract = new web3.eth.Contract(ABI, getContractAddress(chainId));
Practical guidance
  • Keep the ABI constant but the address dynamic per chain.
  • If a contract isn't deployed on a chain, show clear UI and disable that feature.
  • Store the contract map in a single module and import where needed to avoid duplication.
Key Takeaway

Contracts are chain‑specific. Load the correct address for the active chain and reinstantiate contract objects after every chain change.

screens.title: WalletConnector component walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Connecting MetaMask and WalletConnect, switching Sepolia ↔ Mumbai

narration.text: This practical component manages two connection methods: MetaMask via window. ethereum and WalletConnect via @walletconnect/web3-provider. Its key responsibilities are: manage web3 instance, current account, active chain ID, provider type, and a WalletConnect provider instance if used. For MetaMask, call eth_requestAccounts and attach listeners to window. ethereum; for WalletConnect, construct a provider with an Infura ID and RPC map, call enable(), and create a Web3 instance from it. The component should expose connect, disconnect, and switchNetwork functions. Important behaviors include: when accountsChanged returns an empty array, treat it as a disconnect and reset state; when chainChanged fires, convert hex to decimal and reload contract instances using your contract map. When switching networks programmatically, call wallet_switchEthereumChain on the active provider; if error 4902 appears, call wallet_addEthereumChain and then retry. The provided starter code demonstrates these patterns; use it as a scaffold and add clear status messages for the user. A common source of bugs is mixing provider methods between MetaMask and WalletConnect — normalize provider. request calls through a small adapter so your switchNetwork function can call the same code regardless of provider type. After implementing the component, test it by connecting with a mobile wallet and switching between Sepolia and Mumbai to confirm state updates and contract reinitialization.

keyIdea.title: Component responsibilities
keyIdea.text: Manage provider instances, normalize events, support connect/disconnect, perform network switches, and reload contracts when chain changes.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › WalletConnector.js Walkthrough
Starter code
// connectWalletConnect (excerpt)
const provider = new WalletConnectProvider({
  infuraId: INFURA_ID,
  rpc: {
    [SEPOLIA_CHAIN_ID]: NETWORKS[SEPOLIA_CHAIN_ID].rpcUrl,
    [MUMBAI_CHAIN_ID]: NETWORKS[MUMBAI_CHAIN_ID].rpcUrl,
  },
  qrcodeModalOptions: { mobileLinks: ['metamask', 'trust', 'rainbow'] }
});

await provider.enable();
const web3Instance = new Web3(provider);
setWeb3(web3Instance);
setAccount((await web3Instance.eth.getAccounts())[0]);
setChainId(await web3Instance.eth.getChainId());
Important: attach provider.on('accountsChanged', ...), provider.on('chainChanged', ...), and provider.on('disconnect', ...) and remove them on cleanup.
Switch network example
await provider.request({
  method: 'wallet_switchEthereumChain',
  params: [{ chainId: NETWORKS[targetChainId].chainIdHex }]
});
Add a clear status message for: request in progress, user rejected, chain added, or switch successful. This improves user trust and troubleshooting.
Key Takeaway

Use this starter component to normalize providers and test connections by switching between Sepolia and Mumbai while watching state updates and contract reloads.

screens.title: Common mistakes and debugging tips
screens.subtitle: What to avoid and how to surface helpful errors

narration.text: When integrating WalletConnect and multi‑chain support, certain mistakes recur and produce frustrating behavior for users. First, hardcoding chainId or assuming Mainnet will cause features to fail for users on L2s or testnets. Always read chainId dynamically. Second, failing to handle chainChanged leaves your UI out of sync; watch for hex versus decimal chain identifiers and convert when necessary. Third, ignoring disconnect events from WalletConnect will leave stale sessions; always clear local state and prompt the user to reconnect. Fourth, poor error messages make support a nightmare — when a network switch fails, explain why and offer an explicit add network flow rather than a generic failure. For debugging, log provider lifecycle events to the console during development and show a status area in the UI so users can report a clear message. Also test with both MetaMask and a mobile wallet via WalletConnect to exercise both flows. As a final tip, unit test the network mapping module that returns RPC URLs and contract addresses given a chainId to catch mapping errors early. Which of these mistakes could silently break a production feature in your dApp?

keyIdea.title: Pitfalls to avoid
keyIdea.text: Don't hardcode chain assumptions, always handle chainChanged and disconnect, and present clear error messages for network operations.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Common Mistakes
Top mistakes
  • Hardcoding chain assumptions instead of reading chainId.
  • Not handling chainChanged or not converting hex chain IDs.
  • Ignoring disconnect events from WalletConnect.
  • Poorly worded error messages for failed network switches.
Debugging tips
Log provider events and request/response payloads during development so you can trace failures.
Unit test the network configuration mapping to reduce runtime misconfiguration.
Test both connection flows: MetaMask desktop and a mobile wallet via WalletConnect.
Pro tip

Provide a status strip in your app that shows provider, account, chainId, and last provider event to aid troubleshooting during testing and support.

narration.text: Let's recap the essential terms you will reference frequently. WalletConnect is an open protocol that enables encrypted sessions between dApps and wallets, typically established with QR codes or deep links so keys are never exposed to the application. A multi‑chain dApp is designed to work with multiple blockchain networks; it must detect the active chain and adapt RPC endpoints and contract addresses accordingly. The @walletconnect/web3-provider library acts as a bridge, turning WalletConnect sessions into a Web3 provider that your existing Web3. js code can use with minimal changes. Remember these terms and keep the mapping from chainId to network configuration in a single place so your app can adapt reliably when the user switches networks. These core concepts will guide design decisions across UI, state management, and contract interaction patterns.

keyIdea.title: Recap
keyIdea.text: WalletConnect, multi‑chain design, and provider libraries are the foundational pieces for cross‑wallet and cross‑network dApps.

Summary

Keep a single chainId-driven configuration and treat WalletConnect as a remote signer provider to enable cross-device, multi-network interactions.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 2
screens.subtitle: APIs and identifiers to use often

narration.text: A few APIs and identifiers recur while you integrate WalletConnect and multi‑chain features. chainId is the numeric identifier for a network and is authoritative for routing RPCs and contract addresses. wallet_switchEthereumChain is the RPC method you call to request a wallet to change networks; wallet_addEthereumChain is the method to add a new custom network to a wallet when it is not already present. RPC endpoints are how your provider reaches blockchain nodes; keep separate endpoints per chain and include them in your configuration. Finally, handling provider events and disconnects is nonnegotiable — design your app to respond immediately to accountsChanged, chainChanged, and disconnect so UI and contract interactions remain correct. These APIs form the practical toolbox you’ll use every time you implement multi‑chain features. Key Concepts — Part 2 means use chainid, wallet_switchethereumchain, and wallet_addethereumchain together with a per‑chain rpc map to drive multi‑chain behavior.. In practical terms, apis and identifiers to use often. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › APIs & Identifiers
chainId
Unique numeric ID for a blockchain network; use it to select RPCs and contract addresses.
wallet_switchEthereumChain
RPC method to request wallet network changes; pass chainId in hex.
wallet_addEthereumChain
RPC method to prompt the wallet to add a new custom network when not present.
Final summary

Combine chainId-driven configuration, provider methods for switching/adding networks, and robust event handling to build reliable multi‑chain user flows.

ai_generation_note: Create a 15-minute live coding video demonstrating WalletConnect and multi-chain support. Start with a React dApp that connects via MetaMask. Then, integrate `@walletconnect/web3-provider` to offer WalletConnect as an alternative connection method, showing the QR code in the console or a modal. Demonstrate connecting a mobile wallet. Next, implement a network switcher UI element that allows users to switch between Sepolia and Mumbai testnets. Show how to use `wallet_switchEthereumChain` and handle `chainChanged` events to update the dApp's displayed network. Include a split-screen view of the code editor, browser UI, and a mobile wallet emulator or actual phone screen for WalletConnect. Use diagram overlays to explain the WalletConnect flow and multi-chain architecture. End with a 2-question interactive mini-quiz on WalletConnect benefits and multi-chain contract management.
